histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: What is inflammation?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: The tissue response to injury or infection that brings defensive cells and mediators to the site; it is acute or chronic.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: What are the five cardinal signs of inflammation?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Rubor (redness), calor (heat), tumor (swelling), dolor (pain), and functio laesa (loss of function).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: Contrast the timescale and dominant cell of acute vs chronic inflammation.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Acute is rapid (minutes–days) and neutrophil-dominant; chronic is prolonged (weeks–years) with macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: Which cell dominates acute inflammation?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: The neutrophil.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: Which cells dominate chronic inflammation?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells (mononuclear cells).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: What are the two arms of the acute inflammatory response?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Vascular changes (vasodilation and increased permeability) and cellular events (neutrophil recruitment and phagocytosis).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: Describe the vascular changes of acute inflammation.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Transient vasoconstriction, then vasodilation (histamine, NO) causing heat/redness, and increased permeability producing a protein-rich exudate, oedema and vascular stasis.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: List the steps of neutrophil recruitment.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Margination and rolling (selectins) → firm adhesion (integrins binding ICAM-1) → transmigration/diapedesis → chemotaxis to the site.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: Which molecules mediate neutrophil rolling and firm adhesion?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Selectins (E-/P-selectin on endothelium) bind sialyl-Lewis X on leukocyte PSGL-1 for rolling; chemokines then switch leukocyte integrins (LFA-1/Mac-1, CD18) to high affinity for firm binding to endothelial ICAM-1.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: Name important chemotactic agents for neutrophils.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: C5a, leukotriene B4 (LTB4), IL-8, and bacterial products (e.g. N-formyl peptides).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: How does an exudate differ from a transudate?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: An exudate is protein-rich with high specific gravity (from inflammation/increased permeability); a transudate is protein-poor (from hydrostatic/oncotic pressure imbalance).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: What is the neutrophil's role and fate?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: The first responder (a 3–5-lobed segmented cell) that phagocytoses microbes/debris and then dies; accumulated dead neutrophils and debris form pus. (>5 lobes = hypersegmented, seen in B12/folate deficiency.)

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: What is pus?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: A collection of dead neutrophils, necrotic tissue and debris (purulent exudate).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: What are the functions of macrophages in inflammation?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Phagocytosis, antigen presentation, and secretion of cytokines and growth factors; they can become epithelioid and giant cells in granulomas.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: What are Russell bodies?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Cytoplasmic accumulations of immunoglobulin in plasma cells, seen in chronic inflammation.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: Which cells are associated with allergy and parasitic infection?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Eosinophils (with mast cells releasing histamine in allergy).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: What are the causes of chronic inflammation?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Persistent infection (e.g. TB), autoimmunity, foreign material, and prolonged exposure to a toxin/irritant, or unresolved acute inflammation.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: What two processes occur simultaneously in chronic inflammation?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Ongoing tissue destruction and attempted repair (angiogenesis and fibrosis).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: What is granulation tissue?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: New tissue of proliferating capillaries, fibroblasts and inflammatory cells that forms during repair and matures into fibrous scar.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: Name the key chemical mediators of inflammation.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Histamine, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, bradykinin, complement fragments (C3a, C5a), and cytokines (TNF, IL-1, IL-6).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: What does histamine do and where does it come from?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: It causes vasodilation and increased vascular permeability; it is released mainly by mast cells (and basophils).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: Which mediators cause pain and fever?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Prostaglandins (e.g. PGE2), with bradykinin contributing to pain; fever is driven by IL-1, IL-6 and TNF acting via PGE2.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: How do NSAIDs reduce inflammation?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: They inhibit cyclo-oxygenase (COX), reducing prostaglandin synthesis (anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antipyretic). Aspirin inhibits COX irreversibly (and triggers pro-resolving lipoxins); corticosteroids act higher up by inhibiting phospholipase A2, blocking both prostaglandins and leukotrienes.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: What are the possible outcomes of acute inflammation?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Complete resolution, abscess formation, healing with fibrosis/scarring, or progression to chronic inflammation.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: What causes fever in inflammation?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Pyrogenic cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF) raise the hypothalamic set-point via prostaglandin E2.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: What is CRP and what drives it?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: C-reactive protein, an acute-phase protein produced by the liver mainly in response to IL-6; a clinical marker of inflammation.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: What blood-count changes suggest bacterial vs viral infection?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Bacterial infection typically causes neutrophilia; viral infection typically causes lymphocytosis.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: What is the difference between an abscess and cellulitis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: An abscess is a localised collection of pus; cellulitis is a diffuse spreading acute inflammation of the skin/soft tissue.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: What is diapedesis (transmigration)?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: The movement of leukocytes between endothelial cells out of the vessel into the tissue, mediated by PECAM-1.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: Why does tissue become oedematous in acute inflammation?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Vasodilation raises capillary hydrostatic pressure and protein leak through permeable venules lowers plasma oncotic pressure; both shift Starling forces toward filtration, so protein-rich fluid (exudate) accumulates as oedema.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: What is functio laesa?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Loss of function of the inflamed part — the fifth cardinal sign of inflammation.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: How can chronic inflammation arise without a preceding acute phase?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: It can begin insidiously, as in tuberculosis, viral hepatitis, or autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: Outline the arachidonic acid metabolism cascade.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Membrane phospholipids → (phospholipase A2) → arachidonic acid → COX pathway → prostaglandins and thromboxane A2; or lipoxygenase pathway → leukotrienes (LTB4 is chemotactic; LTC4/D4/E4 cause bronchoconstriction and increased permeability).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: Where do corticosteroids and NSAIDs act in the eicosanoid pathway?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Corticosteroids inhibit phospholipase A2 (via annexin-1/lipocortin), blocking both the COX and LOX arms; NSAIDs inhibit only COX (aspirin irreversibly, other NSAIDs reversibly).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: Name the morphological patterns of acute inflammation.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Serous (effusion/blister), fibrinous (e.g. fibrinous pericarditis), suppurative/purulent (abscess), ulcerative, and membranous/pseudomembranous (e.g. C. difficile colitis).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: Contrast M1 and M2 macrophages.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: M1 (classically activated by IFN-γ/LPS) are pro-inflammatory and microbicidal (NO, ROS, IL-1/IL-12/TNF); M2 (alternatively activated by IL-4/IL-13) are anti-inflammatory and promote repair/fibrosis (TGF-β, IL-10, growth factors).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: What are the mechanisms of increased vascular permeability?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Endothelial contraction (histamine/bradykinin/leukotrienes; immediate-transient; venules), direct endothelial injury (burns/severe infection; immediate-sustained), leukocyte-mediated injury (delayed), and increased transcytosis (VEGF-driven).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: What are Light's criteria?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Criteria classifying a pleural effusion as exudative if any of: pleural/serum protein >0.5, pleural/serum LDH >0.6, or pleural LDH greater than two-thirds the upper limit of normal serum LDH.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: What is leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 (LAD-1)?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: A defect in the β2-integrin CD18 causing failed firm adhesion/transmigration: recurrent bacterial infections WITHOUT pus, delayed umbilical cord separation and a marked neutrophilia.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: What is chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: A defect of NADPH oxidase (failed respiratory burst/no H2O2), causing recurrent infection with catalase-positive organisms (S. aureus, Aspergillus, Serratia, Burkholderia) and granulomas; diagnosed with the DHR/nitroblue-tetrazolium test.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: How can chronic inflammation cause amyloidosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Sustained IL-6 raises the acute-phase reactant serum amyloid A (SAA), which can deposit as AA (secondary/reactive) amyloid — a complication of rheumatoid arthritis, TB, chronic osteomyelitis and IBD.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.front: What are specialised pro-resolving mediators (SPMs)?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Infla.back: Lipoxins, resolvins, protectins and maresins — lipid mediators that actively terminate inflammation by stopping neutrophil recruitment and enhancing macrophage clearance of apoptotic cells (efferocytosis).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: What is a granuloma?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: An organised nodular collection of activated (epithelioid) macrophages, often with multinucleate giant cells and a surrounding rim of lymphocytes.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: What type of hypersensitivity reaction underlies granuloma formation?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: Immune granulomas (TB, sarcoid, fungi) are a type IV (delayed, cell-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction; foreign-body granulomas form around inert material without T-cell sensitisation and are non-immune.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: Why do granulomas form?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: To wall off persistent or poorly degradable antigens that ordinary inflammation cannot clear (e.g. TB bacilli, foreign material).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: Which cells drive granuloma formation?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: CD4 Th1 lymphocytes and macrophages (cell-mediated immunity).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: What are the key histological components of a granuloma?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: Epithelioid macrophages, multinucleate giant cells, and a peripheral cuff of lymphocytes (± fibrosis and central necrosis).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: Describe an epithelioid macrophage.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: An activated macrophage with abundant elongated pink cytoplasm resembling epithelium; it is highly secretory but a poor phagocyte.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: Outline the steps of granuloma formation.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: A macrophage engulfs persistent antigen and secretes IL-12, driving CD4 Th1 differentiation → Th1 cells secrete IFN-γ → macrophages activate, become epithelioid and fuse into giant cells → a walled-off granuloma forms, maintained by TNF.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: Which cytokine activates macrophages in a granuloma?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: Interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), released by CD4 Th1 cells.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: Which cytokine maintains granuloma integrity?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: Tumour necrosis factor (TNF).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: Why do anti-TNF drugs risk reactivating tuberculosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: TNF is required to hold granulomas together; blocking it lets granulomas break down and release contained TB bacilli.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: What are multinucleate giant cells?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: Cells formed by the fusion of multiple activated macrophages.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: Describe a Langhans giant cell and its classic association.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: A giant cell with nuclei arranged in a peripheral horseshoe/ring; classically associated with tuberculosis.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: Describe a foreign-body giant cell.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: A giant cell with nuclei scattered randomly, seen around foreign material (often polarisable, e.g. suture, talc).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: Describe a Touton giant cell.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: A giant cell with a ring of nuclei surrounding foamy lipid-laden cytoplasm, seen in fat-rich/xanthomatous lesions.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: What is caseating necrosis and what causes it?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: Central amorphous, eosinophilic 'cheese-like' necrosis within a granuloma; characteristic of tuberculosis and some fungal infections.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: Which conditions cause caseating granulomas?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: Tuberculosis and some fungal infections.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: Which conditions cause non-caseating granulomas?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: Sarcoidosis, Crohn's disease, foreign-body reactions, berylliosis, tuberculoid leprosy, rheumatoid nodules and primary biliary cholangitis. (Cat-scratch disease gives a suppurative granuloma with a neutrophil-rich centre, not a clean non-caseating one.)

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: Which stain identifies acid-fast bacilli in a TB granuloma?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: The Ziehl–Neelsen stain (or the more sensitive fluorescent auramine–rhodamine/auramine-O screen).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: Which stains identify fungi within granulomas?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: Grocott's methenamine silver and PAS stains.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: How can foreign material within a granuloma be identified?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: It is often birefringent (polarisable) under polarised light.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: What are the histological and clinical features of sarcoidosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: Non-caseating granulomas (asteroid/Schaumann bodies, both non-specific), bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, a raised BAL CD4:CD8 ratio (>3.5), raised serum ACE (non-specific), and hypercalcaemia/hypercalciuria from macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase making calcitriol.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: What is a Ghon focus/complex?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: The Ghon focus is a peripheral lung granuloma of primary TB; with involved hilar nodes it forms the Ghon complex.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: What granulomatous features occur in Crohn's disease?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: Non-caseating granulomas in a background of transmural bowel inflammation.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: What is granulomatosis with polyangiitis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: A necrotising granulomatous vasculitis associated with c-ANCA (anti-PR3), affecting the respiratory tract and kidneys.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: What are asteroid and Schaumann bodies?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: Inclusions seen in the giant cells of sarcoidosis (asteroid = star-shaped; Schaumann = laminated calcified); not specific to it.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: Why is a granuloma poor at clearing its antigen?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: Epithelioid macrophages are highly secretory but weak phagocytes, so they contain rather than destroy persistent agents like TB.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: Which infections other than TB cause granulomas?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: Leprosy, fungal infections (histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis), cat-scratch disease, syphilis (gumma) and schistosomiasis.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: What must be done before starting a patient on anti-TNF (biologic) therapy?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: Screen for latent tuberculosis (and treat if positive), because anti-TNF therapy can reactivate TB.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: Why is serum ACE raised in sarcoidosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: The epithelioid macrophages of the granulomas produce angiotensin-converting enzyme; ACE is raised in only ~60% and is neither sensitive nor specific for sarcoidosis.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: What is a syphilitic gumma?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: A granulomatous, rubbery lesion of tertiary syphilis with central necrosis.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: How does granulomatous inflammation differ from ordinary chronic inflammation?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: It is a specific pattern dominated by epithelioid macrophages and giant cells forming discrete nodules, rather than a diffuse mononuclear infiltrate.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: What causes berylliosis and its histology?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: Chronic beryllium exposure causing non-caseating granulomas in the lung, resembling sarcoidosis.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: What is the role of IL-12 in granuloma formation?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: Antigen-laden macrophages secrete IL-12, which drives naïve CD4 T cells to differentiate into Th1 cells; the Th1 cells then produce IFN-γ that activates the macrophages.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: Distinguish immune from foreign-body granulomas.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: Immune (hypersensitivity) granulomas — TB, sarcoid, fungi — are antigen-driven CD4 Th1/type IV reactions; foreign-body granulomas form around inert/poorly-digestible material (suture, talc, keratin) without T-cell involvement.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: What is a suppurative (necrotising) granuloma and its causes?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: A granuloma with a central neutrophil-rich microabscess; caused by cat-scratch disease (Bartonella), lymphogranuloma venereum, Yersinia and some fungi.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: Why is the caseous centre of a TB granuloma poorly penetrated by antibiotics?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: It is hypoxic, acidic and nutrient-poor, favouring bacillary dormancy and limiting drug delivery, so the bacilli are contained rather than killed.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: Explain the mechanism of hypercalcaemia in sarcoidosis.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: Epithelioid macrophages express 1-alpha-hydroxylase, converting 25-OH vitamin D to active 1,25-(OH)2 vitamin D (calcitriol) independent of PTH, increasing gut calcium absorption; hypercalciuria is actually more common than frank hypercalcaemia.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: What is Löfgren syndrome?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: An acute form of sarcoidosis: erythema nodosum + bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy + arthralgia (± fever), which carries a good prognosis and often resolves spontaneously.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: What is Heerfordt syndrome (uveoparotid fever)?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: A form of sarcoidosis with uveitis, parotid gland enlargement, facial nerve palsy and fever.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: What is the bronchoalveolar lavage finding in sarcoidosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: A raised CD4:CD8 T-lymphocyte ratio (typically >3.5) in BAL fluid.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: Name giant cell types beyond Langhans, foreign-body and Touton.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: Osteoclast-type giant cells (bone resorption) and Warthin-Finkeldey giant cells (multinucleate cells seen in measles). Reed-Sternberg cells are NOT granuloma giant cells.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.front: Which fluorescent stain is a sensitive screen for acid-fast bacilli?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Granu.back: Auramine-rhodamine (auramine-O), which is more sensitive than Ziehl-Neelsen for screening for mycobacteria.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What are the two main forms of cell death?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Apoptosis (regulated, programmed, non-inflammatory) and necrosis (uncontrolled, inflammatory).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: Is apoptosis physiological or pathological?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: It can be either — physiological (e.g. embryogenesis, immune selection) or pathological; necrosis is always pathological.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: How do apoptotic and necrotic cells differ in size and membrane?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Apoptotic cells shrink with an intact membrane; necrotic cells swell and their membranes rupture.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: Why does apoptosis cause no inflammation but necrosis does?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: In apoptosis, cell contents are packaged into membrane-bound apoptotic bodies and phagocytosed; in necrosis, membrane rupture spills contents that trigger inflammation.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What are the morphological features of apoptosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation (pyknosis), nuclear fragmentation (karyorrhexis), and membrane-bound apoptotic bodies.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What is the DNA pattern in apoptosis versus necrosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Apoptosis cuts DNA at internucleosomal sites giving a 'ladder'; necrosis produces a random smear.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: Describe the intrinsic (mitochondrial) apoptosis pathway.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Triggered by DNA damage/growth-factor withdrawal. The BCL2-family balance (anti-apoptotic BCL2/BCL-XL/MCL1 vs pro-apoptotic BAX/BAK and BH3-only proteins) determines MOMP; BAX/BAK oligomers release cytochrome c, which forms the apoptosome with APAF-1 and procaspase-9, activating caspase 9.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: Describe the extrinsic (death-receptor) apoptosis pathway.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Ligand binding to death receptors (Fas/FasL, TNF-R) recruits FADD to form the DISC, activating caspase 8; caspase 8 also cleaves BID to tBID, cross-linking to the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: On what do the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converge?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: The executioner caspases (caspase 3, 6 and 7), which dismantle the cell.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What is the role of p53 in cell death?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: After DNA damage it arrests the cycle for repair or triggers apoptosis if the damage is irreparable.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What is the role of BCL2, and its cancer relevance?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: BCL2 is anti-apoptotic; its overexpression (e.g. in follicular lymphoma via t(14;18)) lets cells evade apoptosis.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What causes necrosis at the cellular level?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: ATP depletion and injury causing cell/organelle swelling and membrane rupture with leakage of contents.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: List the progressive nuclear changes of necrosis.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Pyknosis (condensation) → karyorrhexis (fragmentation) → karyolysis (dissolution/fading of the nucleus).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What is coagulative necrosis and where does it occur?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Necrosis with preserved tissue architecture (ghost outlines) from ischaemia; typical of infarcts in most solid organs (heart, kidney).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What is liquefactive necrosis and where does it occur?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Enzymatic digestion of dead tissue into a liquid; seen in brain infarcts and abscesses (pus).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What is caseous necrosis and its classic cause?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Amorphous 'cheese-like' necrosis; classically caused by tuberculosis (and other granulomatous disease).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What is fat necrosis and its causes?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Necrosis of fat with saponification (calcium soaps); seen in acute pancreatitis and traumatic fat necrosis (e.g. breast).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What is fibrinoid necrosis and where is it seen?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Deposition of fibrin and plasma proteins in vessel walls, appearing bright-pink (eosinophilic) on H&E; immune-complex-driven in some vasculitides (e.g. PAN) but from plasma insudation in malignant hypertension/pre-eclampsia.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: Distinguish dry and wet gangrene.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Gangrene is a clinical term, not a distinct mechanism: dry gangrene is coagulative necrosis from ischaemia; wet gangrene adds bacterial infection (liquefactive); gas gangrene is Clostridium infection.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What are Councilman bodies?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Apoptotic hepatocytes seen as eosinophilic globules (also called acidophil bodies), characteristic of viral hepatitis and yellow fever.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: Which type of cell death occurs in a myocardial infarction?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Coagulative necrosis of the ischaemic myocardium.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: Which type of cell death occurs in a cerebral infarct?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Liquefactive necrosis.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: Give examples of physiological apoptosis.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Digit separation in embryogenesis, deletion of self-reactive lymphocytes, endometrial shedding in menstruation, and hormone-dependent tissue involution.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What is the energy requirement of apoptosis versus necrosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Apoptosis is an active, ATP-dependent process; necrosis occurs when ATP is depleted.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: How does the extent of cell death differ between apoptosis and necrosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Apoptosis typically affects single scattered cells; necrosis affects groups of contiguous cells.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What happens to apoptotic bodies?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: They are rapidly phagocytosed by neighbouring cells or macrophages, without provoking inflammation.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: How does defective apoptosis contribute to disease?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Too little apoptosis contributes to cancer and autoimmunity; too much apoptosis contributes to neurodegeneration and ischaemic injury.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What triggers the intrinsic apoptosis pathway?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: DNA damage, growth-factor/hormone withdrawal, and other intracellular stress signals.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What is the significance of cytochrome c release in apoptosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Released from mitochondria, it forms the apoptosome with APAF-1 to activate caspase 9 in the intrinsic pathway.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: Why is coagulative necrosis called 'ghost' necrosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Denatured proteins preserve the cell outlines/tissue architecture for days even though the cells are dead (nuclei lost).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What is saponification in fat necrosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: The formation of calcium soaps when released fatty acids (from lipase action) bind calcium, giving chalky-white deposits.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What newer regulated forms of cell death exist beyond classical apoptosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Necroptosis (RIPK1/RIPK3 → MLKL, caspase-independent), pyroptosis (inflammasome → caspase-1 → gasdermin-D pores + IL-1β/IL-18) and ferroptosis (iron-dependent lipid peroxidation, GPX4 failure) — regulated, often inflammatory forms of necrosis.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What is MOMP and why is it central to intrinsic apoptosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilisation — caused by BAX/BAK oligomers under BH3-only pressure and opposed by BCL2/BCL-XL — releasing cytochrome c to trigger apoptosome/caspase-9 activation; it is the point of no return in intrinsic apoptosis.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What is the apoptosome?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: The wheel-like complex of cytochrome c + APAF-1 + procaspase-9 that assembles in the cytosol during intrinsic apoptosis to activate caspase 9.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: How does caspase 8 link the extrinsic to the intrinsic pathway?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Caspase 8 cleaves BID to truncated tBID, which activates BAX/BAK to cause MOMP, amplifying the death signal through the mitochondria.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What is the significance of phosphatidylserine externalisation?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Apoptotic cells flip phosphatidylserine to the outer membrane leaflet as an "eat-me" signal for macrophage engulfment; it is detected experimentally by annexin V binding.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What marks the transition from reversible to irreversible cell injury?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (MPTP), severe plasma-membrane damage, and massive cytosolic calcium influx.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: Describe necroptosis.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: A regulated, caspase-independent necrosis driven by RIPK1/RIPK3 phosphorylating MLKL, which forms plasma-membrane pores; it is pro-inflammatory (e.g. when caspase-8 is inhibited).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: Describe pyroptosis.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: An inflammatory regulated cell death: inflammasome activation of caspase-1 cleaves gasdermin-D (forming membrane pores) and matures IL-1β/IL-18.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: Describe ferroptosis.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: An iron-dependent regulated necrosis from unchecked lipid peroxidation when the glutathione/GPX4 antioxidant defence fails.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What is oncosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: The pre-lethal cell swelling (from ion-pump failure) that precedes necrosis — the counterpart to the shrinkage seen in apoptosis.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: What is autophagy in the context of cell death?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Lysosomal self-digestion of the cell's own organelles; usually cytoprotective (recycling under stress/starvation) but occasionally acting as a death mechanism.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.front: How does free-radical (ROS) injury damage cells?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Cell.back: Reactive oxygen species (superoxide, H2O2, hydroxyl radical) cause membrane lipid peroxidation, protein oxidation and DNA damage; prominent in ischaemia-reperfusion injury and radiation.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: What is a neoplasm?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: An abnormal, autonomous, uncoordinated tissue growth that persists after the initiating stimulus is removed; it may be benign or malignant.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: How are benign tumours generally named?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: With the suffix '-oma' on the tissue of origin (e.g. adenoma, lipoma, leiomyoma, chondroma).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: How are malignant epithelial and mesenchymal tumours named?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Malignant epithelial tumours are carcinomas; malignant mesenchymal tumours are sarcomas.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: Which '-oma' tumours are exceptions that are actually malignant?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Melanoma, lymphoma, mesothelioma, seminoma, glioma/astrocytoma and hepatoma are malignant despite the '-oma' suffix. (Teratoma may be benign/mature or malignant/immature.)

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: What is a hamartoma?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: A benign, disorganised overgrowth of tissue native to the site — a malformation, not a true neoplasm.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: What is anaplasia?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Loss of cellular differentiation — the hallmark of malignancy, with cells that no longer resemble the tissue of origin.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: List the cytological features of anaplasia/malignancy.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Pleomorphism, hyperchromatic nuclei, a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, prominent nucleoli, and abnormal/frequent mitoses.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: Contrast the growth rate of benign and malignant tumours.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Benign tumours grow slowly with few mitoses; malignant tumours grow rapidly with many, often abnormal, mitoses.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: Contrast the borders of benign and malignant tumours.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Benign tumours are typically well-circumscribed and often encapsulated (expansile); malignant tumours are infiltrative with irregular margins and a desmoplastic stromal reaction. Circumscription favours benignity but is not defining — invasion is the true discriminator.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: What is the single definitive feature that proves a tumour is malignant?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Metastasis — spread to a distant site.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: What is the key histological feature distinguishing invasive carcinoma from carcinoma in situ?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Invasion through the basement membrane (breached in invasive carcinoma; intact in carcinoma in situ).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: What is carcinoma in situ?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Full-thickness dysplasia/malignant change confined by an intact basement membrane, without invasion.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: Why do malignant tumours often show necrosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: They outgrow their blood supply, so central regions become ischaemic and necrotic.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: What are the three main routes of metastatic spread?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Lymphatic (typical of carcinomas), haematogenous (typical of sarcomas, also carcinomas), and transcoelomic (across body cavities).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: Which route do carcinomas versus sarcomas typically favour?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Carcinomas typically spread via lymphatics and sarcomas haematogenously — but renal cell, follicular thyroid, hepatocellular and choriocarcinoma are carcinomas that characteristically spread haematogenously.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: What is transcoelomic spread and give an example?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Spread across a body cavity, e.g. ovarian carcinoma seeding the peritoneal surfaces.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: What are common sites of haematogenous metastasis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Liver, lung, bone and brain.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: How does cancer arise genetically?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: By stepwise accumulation of mutations activating oncogenes and inactivating tumour-suppressor genes (plus DNA-repair defects).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: What is an oncogene, with examples?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: A gene whose gain-of-function mutation promotes cancer, e.g. RAS, MYC and HER2.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: What is a tumour-suppressor gene, with examples?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: A gene whose loss of function permits cancer, e.g. p53, RB and APC.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: Name several hallmarks of cancer.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: The six original: self-sufficiency in growth signals, insensitivity to anti-growth signals, evasion of apoptosis, limitless replication (telomerase), sustained angiogenesis, invasion/metastasis; plus the 2011 additions: genome instability, tumour-promoting inflammation, deregulated energetics (Warburg effect) and avoiding immune destruction.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: What is the difference between grading and staging?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Grade describes how abnormal (differentiated) the tumour cells look; stage describes how far the tumour has spread.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: What does the TNM staging system denote?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: T = primary tumour size/extent, N = regional lymph node involvement, M = distant metastasis.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: Which generally predicts prognosis better — grade or stage?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Stage (the extent of spread) is usually the stronger prognostic factor.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: Which immunostain identifies epithelial (carcinoma) cells?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Cytokeratin.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: Which immunostain identifies mesenchymal cells, and which identifies melanoma?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Vimentin marks mesenchymal cells; S100 marks melanoma (and nerve/Schwann cells).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: Which immunostain identifies lymphoid cells?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: CD45 (leukocyte common antigen).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: What is a paraneoplastic syndrome?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Systemic effects (e.g. hormone secretion causing SIADH, hypercalcaemia or Cushing's) caused by a tumour at a site remote from the tumour or its metastases.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: What is cancer cachexia?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Progressive weight loss, muscle wasting and weakness driven by tumour-derived cytokines (e.g. TNF).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: Give an example of a benign tumour that is dangerous by its location.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: A meningioma — benign but able to compress the brain in a confined space.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: How do tumours evade apoptosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: By overexpressing anti-apoptotic proteins (e.g. BCL2) or losing pro-apoptotic regulators (e.g. p53).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: What is the typical progression sequence to invasive cancer?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Dysplasia → carcinoma in situ (basement membrane intact) → invasive carcinoma (basement membrane breached).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: What is a teratoma?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: A germ-cell tumour containing tissues from all three germ layers; mature teratomas (e.g. ovarian dermoid cyst) are benign, immature teratomas are malignant.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: What does the '-blastoma' suffix denote?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Malignant embryonal tumours of childhood, e.g. nephroblastoma (Wilms), neuroblastoma, retinoblastoma and hepatoblastoma.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: Distinguish hamartoma and choristoma.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: A hamartoma is a disorganised overgrowth of tissue native to the site; a choristoma is normal tissue located at an ectopic site. Neither is a true neoplasm.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: What is the Knudson two-hit hypothesis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Tumour-suppressor genes require inactivation of BOTH alleles to lose function; in familial retinoblastoma one mutant RB allele is inherited (first hit) and a somatic second hit completes it, explaining earlier, bilateral disease.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: Outline the metastatic cascade.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Detachment (E-cadherin loss / epithelial-mesenchymal transition) → invasion of ECM/basement membrane (MMP proteases) → intravasation → survival as circulating emboli → extravasation → colonisation of the new site.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: What is the 'seed and soil' hypothesis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Paget's idea that metastatic organotropism reflects a favourable organ microenvironment ('soil') for particular tumour cells ('seed'), complementing the mechanical/anatomical (drainage) theory.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: What is desmoplasia?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: The dense fibroblastic stromal reaction provoked by an invasive carcinoma, producing the hard 'scirrhous' mass and radiographic spiculation.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: Name common serum tumour markers and their tumours.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: PSA (prostate), AFP (hepatocellular/yolk-sac), CEA (colorectal), CA-125 (ovarian), β-hCG (choriocarcinoma/germ-cell); used mainly for monitoring, not screening.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: Name oncogenic viruses/microbes and their cancers.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: HPV (cervical/oropharyngeal SCC), EBV (Burkitt, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Hodgkin), HBV/HCV (hepatocellular carcinoma), HTLV-1 (adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma), HHV-8 (Kaposi sarcoma), H. pylori (gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: What is the adenoma-carcinoma sequence?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: The stepwise colorectal model in which normal mucosa progresses through adenoma to carcinoma via accumulated mutations (APC → KRAS → p53), showing that some benign precursor lesions can become malignant.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.front: What is a sentinel lymph node biopsy?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Neopl.back: Biopsy of the first lymph node draining a tumour (localised by dye/radiotracer); if negative, further nodes are usually spared. Widely used in breast cancer and melanoma.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: What is metaplasia?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: The (potentially reversible) replacement of one differentiated tissue type by another, as an adaptation to stress, via reprogramming of tissue stem/reserve cells — mature cells do not directly transdifferentiate.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: What is dysplasia?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Disordered epithelial growth with cytological atypia and architectural disarray, but without invasion (basement membrane intact); it is pre-malignant.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: How does metaplasia differ conceptually from dysplasia?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Metaplasia is an adaptive change (via stem-cell reprogramming) to another normal mature tissue type, potentially reversible; dysplasia is disordered, atypical, pre-malignant growth.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: List the main cellular adaptations to stress.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Hypertrophy (bigger cells), hyperplasia (more cells), atrophy (smaller/fewer cells), and metaplasia (change of cell type).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: What is Barrett's oesophagus and its cause?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Metaplasia of oesophageal squamous epithelium to metaplastic columnar epithelium from chronic acid reflux. The UK/BSG definition requires only a columnar-lined oesophagus; the US/CAP definition also requires goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: What metaplasia occurs in the bronchi of smokers?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium changes to stratified squamous epithelium (losing the protective cilia).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: What metaplasia occurs at the cervical transformation zone?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Columnar epithelium undergoes squamous metaplasia (a normal physiological process).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: What gastric metaplasia is associated with H. pylori?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Intestinal metaplasia — replacement of gastric epithelium by intestinal-type epithelium with goblet cells.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: What metaplasia can occur in the bladder and its triggers?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Transitional epithelium can undergo squamous (schistosomiasis, stones) or glandular metaplasia.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: What is myositis ossificans an example of?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Mesenchymal metaplasia — connective tissue changing into bone.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: Why can metaplasia be harmful despite being adaptive?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: It often sacrifices the original protective function (e.g. loss of cilia in the bronchi) and provides a substrate for dysplasia if the stress persists.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: Is metaplasia reversible?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: In principle yes — if the stimulus is removed — but many established metaplasias (Barrett's, gastric intestinal metaplasia) persist and rarely fully regress.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: What are the cytological features of dysplasia?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Nuclear pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, increased/abnormal mitoses, and loss of polarity and maturation.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: What architectural feature is retained in dysplasia that is lost in invasive carcinoma?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: An intact basement membrane — dysplasia does not invade.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: How is dysplasia graded?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: As low-grade or high-grade (severe) dysplasia, according to the degree of atypia and architectural disorder.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: What is high-grade dysplasia equivalent to?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Carcinoma in situ — full-thickness dysplastic change with an intact basement membrane (the two overlap and are often used interchangeably, though "CIS" is avoided at glandular/GI sites).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: Is dysplasia reversible?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Low-grade dysplasia may reverse if the stimulus is removed, but higher grades carry an increasing risk of progression to invasive cancer.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: State the sequence of progression from normal epithelium to cancer.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Normal → metaplasia → dysplasia → carcinoma in situ → invasive carcinoma.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: What is the key irreversible step in this sequence?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Invasion through the basement membrane (invasive carcinoma); metaplasia and dysplasia are potentially reversible.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: How does Barrett's oesophagus relate to cancer?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: The intestinal metaplasia can develop dysplasia and progress to oesophageal adenocarcinoma, so it is monitored by surveillance endoscopy.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: What is CIN?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia — HPV-driven dysplasia of the cervix graded CIN 1–3, detected by cervical smear.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: What malignancy does bronchial squamous metaplasia/dysplasia lead to?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: What is actinic keratosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: A sun-induced dysplasia of the epidermis that is premalignant and can progress to cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: What is leukoplakia?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: A white oral mucosal patch that cannot be rubbed off — a CLINICAL diagnosis of exclusion (biopsy needed; may show anything from hyperkeratosis to carcinoma). Its red counterpart, erythroplakia, carries a much higher risk of dysplasia/SCC.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: Why is recognition of metaplasia/dysplasia clinically important?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: It allows screening and surveillance (e.g. cervical smears, Barrett's endoscopy) to intervene before invasive cancer develops.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: How does dysplasia differ from anaplasia?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Dysplasia is disordered but non-invasive pre-malignant growth; anaplasia is the marked loss of differentiation characteristic of established malignancy.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: What distinguishes carcinoma in situ from invasive carcinoma?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Carcinoma in situ is confined by an intact basement membrane, whereas invasive carcinoma has breached it.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: Does metaplasia itself represent cancer?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: No — metaplasia is a benign adaptive change, though it can be a precursor state if the stress persists.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: What cell provides the source for metaplastic change?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Tissue stem cells, which are reprogrammed to differentiate along a different pathway.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: What is the difference between hyperplasia and dysplasia?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Hyperplasia is an orderly increase in cell number; dysplasia is a disordered increase with cytological atypia (pre-malignant).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: Which metaplasia predisposes to adenocarcinoma versus squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Barrett's (glandular/intestinal) metaplasia predisposes to adenocarcinoma; the native squamous epithelium relates to squamous cell carcinoma.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: What is the typical fate of untreated high-grade dysplasia?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: A significant proportion progresses to invasive carcinoma, which is why it is treated/excised.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: What is CDX2 and its role in metaplasia?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: The master transcription factor driving intestinal (columnar/goblet) differentiation; its ectopic expression underlies intestinal metaplasia in Barrett's oesophagus and gastric intestinal metaplasia.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: Which vitamin deficiency causes squamous metaplasia?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Vitamin A (retinoic acid) deficiency causes squamous metaplasia of respiratory, urinary and glandular/conjunctival epithelium (xerophthalmia/keratomalacia); retinoids can reverse it.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: Give an example of a benign metaplasia that is NOT premalignant.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Apocrine metaplasia of the breast — a benign change; it is the dysplasia that may later arise, not the metaplasia itself, that carries cancer risk.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: What is myeloid metaplasia?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Extramedullary haematopoiesis — blood-cell production appearing outside the marrow (e.g. in the spleen/liver in myelofibrosis) — a form of metaplasia.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: Why can permanent tissues not undergo hyperplasia?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Cardiac muscle, skeletal muscle and neurons are permanent (post-mitotic) cells; they cannot divide, so they adapt to increased demand only by hypertrophy.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: How reliable is dysplasia grading, and what helps?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Interobserver reproducibility (especially low- vs high-grade in Barrett's/IBD) is poor; p53 immunostaining and DNA aneuploidy/flow cytometry serve as objective adjunct markers of neoplastic progression.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: Distinguish leukoplakia from erythroplakia.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Both are clinical descriptors of oral mucosal patches (diagnoses of exclusion needing biopsy): leukoplakia (white) has variable, often low dysplasia risk; erythroplakia (red) carries a much higher risk of dysplasia/invasive SCC.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.front: Why is the cervical transformation zone especially prone to dysplasia?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Metap.back: Its actively dividing metaplastic (immature squamous) cells are the site where high-risk HPV integrates, driving CIN — the metaplasia provides the susceptible substrate.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: What are the two ways tissue heals after injury?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Regeneration (restoring normal tissue) and repair by fibrosis (replacement with a collagen scar).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: What determines whether tissue regenerates or scars?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: The regenerative capacity of the cells (labile/stable vs permanent) and whether the connective-tissue framework is intact.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: Define labile cells and give examples.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Continuously dividing cells that regenerate well — epidermis, gastrointestinal epithelium and bone marrow.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: Define stable cells and give examples.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Quiescent cells that can re-enter the cell cycle to divide if needed — liver, kidney tubules and fibroblasts; they regenerate if the framework is intact.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: Define permanent cells and give examples.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Non-dividing cells — neurons and cardiac muscle — that cannot regenerate and heal by scar. Skeletal muscle is often grouped here but has limited regeneration via satellite (Pax7) cells; large defects still scar.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: Why does a healed myocardial infarct become a scar rather than new muscle?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Cardiac myocytes are permanent cells that cannot regenerate, so the damaged area heals by fibrosis.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: What is granulation tissue?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Early repair tissue of new capillaries (angiogenesis), proliferating fibroblasts, loose extracellular matrix and inflammatory cells; it looks pink and granular.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: What is the role of myofibroblasts in healing?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: They contract the wound to reduce its size (wound contraction); they are identified by their expression of alpha-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: What is the sequence of wound healing?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Haemostasis → inflammation → proliferation (granulation, angiogenesis, re-epithelialisation) → remodelling/maturation (scar).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: How does collagen change during wound remodelling?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Early type III collagen (in granulation tissue) is replaced by stronger type I collagen as the scar matures.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: How strong does a healed wound eventually become?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: About 10% at one week (suture-removal time), rising through ~3 months to a plateau of roughly 70–80% — it never regains 100% of original strength.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: Contrast healing by primary and secondary intention.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Primary intention: clean, apposed edges with little tissue loss, fast healing and a small scar. Secondary intention: large/gaping wounds with abundant granulation, wound contraction and a larger scar.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: Which growth factor drives angiogenesis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: Which growth factor recruits fibroblasts and smooth muscle?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: Which cytokine is the key driver of fibrosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: What is fibrosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Excessive deposition of collagen that replaces normal tissue and impairs organ function, resulting from chronic injury/inflammation.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: Give examples of pathological fibrosis.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Liver cirrhosis (stellate cells), pulmonary fibrosis, cardiac fibrosis after MI, and chronic kidney disease.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: Which cells drive hepatic fibrosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Activated hepatic stellate (Ito) cells — normally vitamin A-storing — which lose their retinoid droplets and transdifferentiate into collagen-secreting myofibroblasts.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: What is a hypertrophic scar?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Excess collagen deposition confined within the original wound margins.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: What is a keloid?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Excess disorganised collagen (raised type I:III ratio) extending beyond the original wound margins; there is a genetic/ethnic predisposition (pigmented skin; sternum, earlobe, deltoid) and a tendency to recur after excision.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: What is a wound contracture?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Excessive, deforming contraction of a wound (e.g. across a joint after a burn) due to myofibroblast activity.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: What is wound dehiscence?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Rupture/separation of a wound, e.g. of a surgical incision.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: List factors that impair wound healing.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Diabetes, corticosteroids, infection, ischaemia/poor perfusion, poor nutrition (protein, vitamin C, zinc), foreign body, old age and certain drugs (e.g. chemotherapy).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: Why does vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) impair healing?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Vitamin C (with Fe2+) is the cofactor for prolyl/lysyl hydroxylase, which hydroxylates proline and lysine to stabilise the collagen triple helix; without it, weak undersynthesised collagen causes poor healing and bleeding. (The covalent cross-linking step is done by lysyl oxidase, a copper-dependent enzyme.)

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: Why do corticosteroids impair wound healing?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: They inhibit inflammation, fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: Which stain highlights collagen/fibrosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Masson's trichrome (collagen stains blue/green); reticulin stains can also demonstrate the framework.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: What histological features distinguish a mature scar from granulation tissue?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: A mature scar is dense collagen with few cells and vessels, whereas granulation tissue is cellular and vascular with fibroblasts and capillaries.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: What does angiogenesis contribute to repair?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: It forms new blood vessels that supply oxygen and nutrients to the healing tissue.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: Why is an intact basement membrane/framework important for regeneration?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: It provides the scaffold that allows regenerating cells to reconstitute normal architecture; if destroyed, healing occurs by scarring instead.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: What role do macrophages play in repair?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: They clear debris and secrete growth factors (e.g. TGF-β, PDGF, VEGF) that drive angiogenesis and fibroblast activity.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: Why does diabetes impair wound healing?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Microvascular disease, poor perfusion, neuropathy and impaired immune/fibroblast function slow healing and increase infection risk.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: What is the difference between a hypertrophic scar and a keloid in behaviour?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: A hypertrophic scar stays within the wound and may regress; a keloid extends beyond the wound margins and tends to persist/recur.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: Which cells allow skeletal muscle to regenerate?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Satellite cells — quiescent Pax7-positive myogenic progenitors beneath the basal lamina — repair limited skeletal muscle injury; extensive damage still heals by scar.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: Which enzyme cross-links collagen, and what cofactor does it need?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Lysyl oxidase, a copper-dependent enzyme, forms the covalent cross-links between collagen molecules; copper deficiency (or lathyrism) weakens collagen.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: What is the wound-strength recovery timeline?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Roughly 10% of normal at 1 week, rising over ~3 months to a plateau of about 70–80%; a scar never regains full original strength.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: What is the role of MMPs and TIMPs in remodelling?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Matrix metalloproteinases (zinc-dependent) degrade and remodel collagen (type III → type I turnover), balanced by their inhibitors, the tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: How does the liver regenerate after injury?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Mainly by compensatory hyperplasia of mature hepatocytes re-entering the cell cycle; hepatic progenitor (oval) cells are recruited only after massive/submassive necrosis.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: What is the provisional matrix in wound healing?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: The fibrin clot with fibronectin, which forms a scaffold guiding the migration of fibroblasts and endothelial cells before collagen is deposited.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: How does hypoxia drive angiogenesis in repair?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Hypoxia stabilises HIF-1α, which up-regulates VEGF; VEGF then drives new-vessel formation by endothelial sprouting.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: What histological features distinguish a scar from normal dermis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: A scar is dense, disorganised collagen lacking adnexal structures (hair follicles, sweat/sebaceous glands) and elastic tissue.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: Distinguish granulation tissue from a granuloma.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Granulation tissue is repair tissue (new capillaries + fibroblasts + inflammatory cells); a granuloma is an organised nodule of epithelioid macrophages in chronic (type IV) inflammation — despite the similar names they are unrelated.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.front: Which collagen type forms the basement membrane?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Fibro.back: Type IV collagen (a sheet-like network), distinct from type III (reticular, early granulation) and type I (mature scar/most tissues) fibrillar collagens.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: What two processes dominate vascular pathology and its major consequences?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: Atherosclerosis (chronic arterial intimal disease) and thrombosis (intravascular clot); together they cause ischaemia and infarction (MI, stroke).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: What is atherosclerosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: A chronic inflammatory disease of the INTIMA of large and medium arteries characterised by plaques (atheromas); it is one type of arteriosclerosis (the umbrella term that also covers Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis and arteriolosclerosis).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: Outline the 'response to injury' pathogenesis of atherosclerosis.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: Endothelial injury → LDL enters the intima and is oxidised → macrophages take up oxLDL via unregulated scavenger receptors → foam cells → fatty streak → (with T-cell inflammation and PDGF) smooth muscle cells migrate from the media and proliferate → fibrous plaque with a necrotic lipid core.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: What is a foam cell?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: A lipid-laden macrophage that has ingested oxidised LDL in the arterial intima.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: What is the earliest visible lesion of atherosclerosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: The fatty streak (lipid-laden foam cells in the intima) — the earliest lesion, and potentially reversible.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: Describe the structure of an atherosclerotic plaque.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: A fibrous cap (smooth muscle and collagen) overlying a necrotic lipid core (cholesterol clefts, foam cells and debris), sometimes with calcification.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: What are cholesterol clefts?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: Needle-shaped empty spaces in the necrotic core where cholesterol crystals dissolved during tissue processing.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: Which arteries are most affected by atherosclerosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: The abdominal aorta, coronary arteries, popliteal arteries, carotids and circle of Willis.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: Contrast stable and vulnerable (unstable) plaques.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: Stable plaques have a thick fibrous cap and small lipid core (stable angina); vulnerable plaques have a thin cap and large lipid core prone to rupture, causing acute coronary syndrome.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: What are the complications of atherosclerosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: Stenosis/ischaemia, plaque rupture with thrombosis (MI, stroke), aneurysm formation, embolism and calcification.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: List the modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors for atherosclerosis.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: Modifiable: smoking, hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidaemia, obesity. Non-modifiable: age, male sex, family history.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: What is Virchow's triad?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: The three contributors to thrombosis: endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow (stasis or turbulence), and hypercoagulability.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: How does an arterial thrombus differ from a venous thrombus?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: Arterial thrombi form in high flow on ruptured plaques and are pale/platelet-rich (with prominent lines of Zahn); venous thrombi form in stasis and are red/RBC-rich.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: What are lines of Zahn and their significance?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: Alternating pale (platelet/fibrin) and red (red-cell) layers within a thrombus, indicating antemortem formation in flowing blood; they need flow, so are prominent in arterial/cardiac thrombi but often inapparent in venous (stasis) thrombi.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: How is an antemortem thrombus distinguished from a post-mortem clot?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: A thrombus is attached to the vessel wall and shows lines of Zahn; a post-mortem clot is unattached, gelatinous ('chicken-fat/currant-jelly') and lacks lines of Zahn.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: What are the possible fates of a thrombus?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: Propagation, embolisation, dissolution (fibrinolysis), or organisation with recanalisation.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: What is an embolism?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: A detached intravascular solid, liquid or gaseous mass carried by the blood to a distant site.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: What is the commonest type of embolism?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: Thromboembolism — most often a venous thrombus embolising to the lungs (pulmonary embolism).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: Give examples of non-thrombotic emboli.
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: Fat (long-bone fractures), air, amniotic fluid, septic, tumour and cholesterol emboli.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: What is a pulmonary embolism and its usual source?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: Occlusion of a pulmonary artery by an embolus, usually from a deep vein thrombosis of the legs.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: What is an infarction?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: Ischaemic necrosis of tissue due to occlusion of its blood (or venous) supply.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: Which type of necrosis occurs in most infarcts, and what is the brain's exception?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: Most infarcts show coagulative necrosis; the brain undergoes liquefactive necrosis.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: Where do white (anaemic) infarcts occur and why?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: In solid organs with an end-arterial supply — heart, kidney, spleen — where little collateral blood enters the dead area.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: Where do red (haemorrhagic) infarcts occur and why?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: In loose tissues or organs with a dual/collateral supply (lung, bowel) or with venous occlusion, allowing blood to seep into the infarct.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: What is a paradoxical embolism?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: A venous embolus that passes through a cardiac septal defect into the arterial circulation, causing systemic embolism.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: How does plaque rupture cause a myocardial infarction?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: Rupture exposes the thrombogenic core, triggering platelet aggregation and thrombosis that acutely occludes the coronary artery.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: What is a fat embolism syndrome?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: Fat globules (usually from long-bone fractures) embolising to the lungs and brain, causing the triad of respiratory distress, neurological confusion and a petechial rash — characteristically 24–72 hours after the injury.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: Why are antiplatelet drugs used for arterial disease and anticoagulants for venous?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: Arterial thrombi are platelet-rich (antiplatelets), whereas venous thrombi are fibrin/coagulation-driven (anticoagulants).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: How do statins help in atherosclerosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: They lower LDL cholesterol and stabilise plaques (reducing lipid core and inflammation), lowering the risk of rupture.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: What is an aneurysm and how does atherosclerosis cause it?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: An abnormal localised dilatation of a vessel. Abdominal aortic aneurysm (infrarenal) results from chronic inflammation and MMP-mediated destruction of the medial elastin/collagen (smoking is the strongest risk factor); atherosclerosis is contributory, not simply "weakening the media".

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: What is peripheral arterial disease?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: Atherosclerotic stenosis of limb arteries causing intermittent claudication and, if severe, critical limb ischaemia.

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: What inherited condition commonly causes hypercoagulability?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: Factor V Leiden (activated protein C resistance).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: What are the three forms of arteriosclerosis?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: Atherosclerosis (intimal plaques of large/medium arteries); Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis (calcification of the media of muscular arteries, elderly, does not narrow the lumen); and arteriolosclerosis (small arteries/arterioles) — hyaline (benign hypertension/diabetes) and hyperplastic "onion-skin" (malignant hypertension).

histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.front: From where do the smooth muscle cells of the fibrous cap originate?
histology__PATHOLOGICAL HISTOLOGY__Vascu.back: They migrate from the media into the intima (driven by PDGF and other growth factors) and secrete collagen to form the cap.
